title: Rethinking ImageNet Pre-training
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)

problem.summary: The field assumes detectors must be fine-tuned from ImageNet-pretrained networks and that from-scratch training is non-trivial, while the actual detection gains from ever-larger pre-training sets are small and diminishing. Comparisons are also confounded because the cost of ImageNet pre-training is usually ignored and short schedules hide what from-scratch training really needs.
statements: Most modern object detectors follow the pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm, and the belief that training from scratch is non-trivial became conventional wisdom.
Improvements on object detection from large-scale pre-training are relatively small (about +1.5 AP on COCO with 3000x larger pre-training data) and the marginal benefit diminishes rapidly.
Controlled comparisons using short training schedules can veil the true behavior of training from random initialization because the cost of ImageNet pre-training is often ignored.
Prior from-scratch detectors (DSOD, DetNet, CornerNet) rely on detection-specific architectures, leaving the role of pre-training on unspecialized architectures untested.

evidence.quote: As modern object detectors [9, 15, 8, 36, 35, 28, 26, 13] evolved under the pre-training paradigm, the belief that training from scratch is non-trivial became conventional wisdom.
the improvements on object detection are relatively small (on the scale of +1.5 AP on COCO with 3000× larger pre-training data [30]).

However, in [41, 25, 22] there is little evidence that these specialized architectures are required for models to be trained from scratch.

background.summary: The work builds on the R-CNN/Fast R-CNN/Faster R-CNN lineage of fine-tuned detectors, on Mask R-CNN + FPN + Detectron as the experimental baseline, on GroupNorm/SyncBN for small-batch normalization, and on earlier from-scratch work (DSOD, DetNet, CornerNet) plus early analyses showing scratch training can reach ~90% of fine-tuning accuracy.

Our work demonstrates that it is often possible to match fine-tuning accuracy when training from scratch even without making any architectural specializations.

solution.summary: The paper's method is a controlled experimental recipe: train standard Mask R-CNN (ResNet/ResNeXt + FPN) from random initialization with only two necessary changes - appropriate normalization (GroupNorm or SyncBN, or normalized initialization for VGG) and training schedules long enough (5x/6x) to compensate for the missing pre-training - while keeping architectures and hyper-parameters identical to the fine-tuned counterparts.
solution.approach: Train unmodified baseline detectors from random initialization with batch-size-independent normalization and 5x-6x longer schedules, then compare against identical ImageNet-pretrained systems under controlled hyper-parameters.
components: GroupNorm or Synchronized BatchNorm replacing all frozen-BN layers
normalized (MSRA) initialization enabling VGG nets to train without BN/GN
extended training schedules (2x up to 6x, and 9x/11x in enhanced settings)
identical architectures and hyper-parameters for scratch and pre-trained runs
sample-count analysis (images, instances, pixels) to argue fairness of longer training
evaluations across bbox AP, mask AP, keypoint AP, augmentation and cascade variants

evidence.quote: We report competitive results on object detection and instance segmentation on the COCO dataset using standard models trained from random initialization.

We find that there is no fundamental obstacle preventing us from training from scratch, if: (i) we use normalization techniques appropriately for optimization, and (ii) we train the models sufficiently long to compensate for the lack of pre-training
We describe the only two modifications that we find to be necessary, related to model normalization and training length
Our experiments show that both GN and SyncBN can enable detection models to train from scratch.
we argue that models trained from scratch must be trained for longer than typical fine-tuning schedules.

experiments.summary: Mask R-CNN with ResNet-50/101/ResNeXt-152 and VGG-16 backbones is trained on COCO train2017 from random init versus ImageNet init across 2x-6x schedules and evaluated on val2017 (bbox, mask, keypoint AP), plus reduced-data regimes (35k, 10k, 3.5k, 1k images) and PASCAL VOC; the best scratch model is also submitted to the COCO 2018 challenge.

limitations.summary: From-scratch training needs roughly three times more target-task iterations (extra compute), it breaks down below roughly 10k COCO images and on PASCAL VOC, and it is impossible with vanilla BatchNorm under typical detection batch sizes unless GN/SyncBN or special initialization is used.
items: Requires much longer training: 540k iterations (6x schedule), and up to 9x/11x in enhanced or VGG settings.
Breaks down in very small data regimes: with 1k COCO images, scratch reaches only 3.5-5.4 AP vs 9.9 AP with pre-training; the breakdown point lies between 3.5k and 10k COCO images.
On PASCAL VOC, training from scratch gives 77.6 mAP versus 82.7 mAP with ImageNet pre-training and never catches up.
Small batch sizes degrade BatchNorm, so frozen-BN style training from scratch is invalid and normalization must be changed.
Training for longer on the small learning rate stage often leads to overfitting.

evidence.quote: the model with ImageNet pre-training has 9.9 AP vs. the from scratch model’s 3.5 AP.
Its counterpart trained from scratch in VOC has 77.6 mAP at 144k iterations and does not catch up even training longer.
We find that training longer for the first (large) learning rate is useful, but training for longer on small learning rates often leads to overfitting.
small batch sizes severely degrade the accuracy of BN [19, 34, 48].

futureDirections.direction: Prefer collecting and training on target-task data over ever-larger generic pre-training sets as compute and data grow.
futureDirections.quote: looking forward, when the community will proceed with more data and faster computation, our study suggests that collecting data and training on the target tasks is a solution worth considering

futureDirections.direction: Shift data-collection effort into the target domain if classification-level pre-training gains keep diminishing.
futureDirections.quote: If the gain of large-scale classification-level pre-training becomes exponentially diminishing [44, 30], it would be more effective to collect data in the target domain.

futureDirections.direction: Re-evaluate self-supervised and other pre-trained features against random-initialization baselines.
futureDirections.quote: our study suggests that the community should be more careful when evaluating pre-trained features
